title: Splitting an extension with a one-dimensional additive subgroup kernel
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups below are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups and closed immersions are as in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup, def-weil-closed-immersion]. Let $M$ be a finitely generated abelian group and let $D=\operatorname{Spec}k[M]$, where $k[M]$ has basis $e_a$, multiplication $e_ae_b=e_{a+b}$, comultiplication $e_a\mapsto e_a\otimes e_a$, counit $e_a\mapsto1$, and antipode $e_a\mapsto e_{-a}$. Let $\chi:D\to\mathbf G_m$ be a group-scheme homomorphism, and let $N\subseteq\mathbf G_a$ be a closed subgroup scheme stable under scalar multiplication by $\chi$. Here $\mathbf G_a(R)=(R,+)$ and $\mathbf G_m(R)=R^\times$ for a commutative $k$-algebra $R$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $i:N\hookrightarrow E$ be a closed normal subgroup and let $q:E\to D$ identify $D$ with the fppf sheaf quotient $E/i(N)$, with scheme-theoretic kernel $i(N)$. The quotient is the sheafification of $R\mapsto E(R)/i(N)(R)$ for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings. Assume that on every commutative $k$-algebra $R$, every $e\in E(R)$ and $x\in N(R)\subseteq R$ satisfy
$$e\,i_R(x)\,e^{-1}=i_R\bigl(\chi_R(q_R(e))x\bigr).$$
Then there is a homomorphism of $k$-group schemes $s:D\to E$ with $q\circ s=\operatorname{id}_D$. No smoothness or connectedness is assumed for $N,E,D$.

source.place: Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319 (vanishing of the extension group for a subgroup of the additive group with a linear multiplicative-type action); application to the pullback extension in Theorem 16.26(a), printed pp.332--333.

proof.text:
Form the affine finite-type group $H=\mathbf G_a\rtimes E$ with multiplication $(v,e)(w,f)=(v+\chi(q(e))w,ef)$ and inverse $(v,e)^{-1}=(-\chi(q(e))^{-1}v,e^{-1})$. These are scheme morphisms and satisfy the group axioms by the character identity. The graph $K=\{(-x,i(x)):x\in N\}$ is a closed subgroup isomorphic to $N$. Its normality is the explicit identity
$$(v,e)(-x,i(x))(v,e)^{-1}=(-\chi(q(e))x,i(\chi(q(e))x)).$$
Stability of $N$ makes the right side an element of $K$ on every algebra. Apply the affine normal quotient theorem to obtain the affine finite-type group $F=H/K$ and its fppf quotient map. Write $[v,e]$ for a local representative; the brackets do not assert existence of a representative over the original algebra.

source.place: Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319; concretization of its additive-kernel reduction, using Example 2.72 (p.61), Proposition 15.31 (p.318), and Exercise 14-3(a) (p.301).

proof.text: The homomorphisms $u:\mathbf G_a\to F$, $v\mapsto[v,1]$, $j:E\to F$, $e\mapsto[0,e]$, and $r:F\to D$, $[v,e]\mapsto q(e)$ satisfy $rj=q$. The formula for $r$ is invariant under $K$, hence descends by the defining quotient-sheaf universal property. Both $u$ and $j$ are monomorphisms: fppf locally membership of $(v,1)$ or $(0,e)$ in $K$ forces respectively $x=0$ or $x=0$, and then $v=0$ or $e=1$. If $q(e)=1$, write $e=i(x)$; the relation $[v,i(x)]=[v+x,1]$ identifies $\ker r$ with $u(\mathbf G_a)$. Local surjectivity of $q$ shows that $r$ is locally surjective as a sheaf map. Thus $D=F/u(\mathbf G_a)$ as fppf sheaves. The kernel is a closed normal subgroup, and the quotient theorem says that $r$ is a faithfully flat finitely presented $\mathbf G_a$-torsor. Conjugation on its kernel is $f u(v)f^{-1}=u(\chi(r(f))v)$, as follows locally from the multiplication in $H$.

source.place: Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319; concretization of its additive-kernel reduction, using Example 2.72 (p.61), Proposition 15.31 (p.318), and Exercise 14-3(a) (p.301).

proof.text: Here is the affine additive-torsor argument, with no new torsor lemma. Put $B=k[M]=\mathcal O(D)$ and $C=\mathcal O(F)$; $B\to C$ is faithfully flat by the preceding step. The tautological section $t_C$ over $\operatorname{Spec}C$ has two pullbacks related uniquely by $t_2=u(z)t_1$, with $z\in C\otimes_B C$. On triple overlaps $z_{13}=z_{12}+z_{23}$. Amitsur exactness for $B\to C$ with module $B$ gives $w\in C$ with $z=1\otimes w-w\otimes1$. Therefore $u(-w)t_C$ agrees on the double overlap. To descend it, use affineness: its coordinate algebra map $\mathcal O(F)\to C$ has image in the equalizer of $C\rightrightarrows C\otimes_B C$, which is $B$ by the same exactness. Its unique factorization into $B$ preserves sums, products and scalars since $B\to C$ is injective. It defines a scheme section $t:D\to F$ of $r$. Translate $t$ on the left by $t(1)^{-1}\in u(k)$ so that $t(1)=1$.

source.place: Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319; concretization of its additive-kernel reduction, using Example 2.72 (p.61), Proposition 15.31 (p.318), and Exercise 14-3(a) (p.301).

proof.text:
Define the regular function $c:D\times D\to\mathbf G_a$ by $t(x)t(y)=u(c(x,y))t(xy)$. The torsor identity supplies $c$ as a scheme morphism, not merely as a rule on field-valued points. Associativity and the preceding conjugation formula give
$$c(x,y)+c(xy,z)=\chi(x)c(y,z)+c(x,yz).$$
Let $\lambda:B\to k$ extract the coefficient of $e_0$, and put $b=(\operatorname{id}_B\otimes\lambda)c\in B$. Since $\Delta(e_a)=e_a\otimes e_a$, applying $\lambda$ in the second variable of $h(xy)$ gives the constant $\lambda(h)$ for any $h\in B$. Apply $\lambda$ in the $z$ variable of the displayed identity to obtain
$$c(x,y)+b(xy)=\chi(x)b(y)+b(x).$$
Consequently $\sigma(d)=u(-b(d))t(d)$ satisfies $\sigma(x)\sigma(y)=\sigma(xy)$ and $r\sigma=1_D$. The multiplicative identity also forces $\sigma(1)=1$. This calculation uses the group-algebra basis, including when $D$ is nonreduced; it does not average geometric points.

source.place: Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319; concretization of its additive-kernel reduction, using Example 2.72 (p.61), Proposition 15.31 (p.318), and Exercise 14-3(a) (p.301).

proof.text: If $N=\mathbf G_a$, every $[v,e]$ is locally $[0,i(v)e]$. The monomorphism $j$ is therefore an isomorphism of the represented quotient sheaves, so $j^{-1}\sigma$ is the required section of $q$. Otherwise apply the monic additive-polynomial quotient node to the proper subgroup $N$, with $G=D$ and $\eta=\chi$. Obtain its polynomial $P$ of positive degree $n$, kernel $N$, and identity $P(\chi(d)v)=\chi(d)^nP(v)$. Put $\psi=\chi^n$.

source.place: Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319; concretization of its additive-kernel reduction, using Example 2.72 (p.61), Proposition 15.31 (p.318), and Exercise 14-3(a) (p.301).

proof.text:
In the proper-subgroup case the rule $a([v,e])=P(v)$ descends to a scheme morphism $a:F\to\mathbf G_a$: replacing $(v,e)$ by $(v,e)(-x,i(x))$ replaces $v$ by $v-\chi(q(e))x$, whose $P$-value is unchanged. The quotient universal property gives descent, and the multiplication formula gives
$$a(ff')=a(f)+\psi(r(f))a(f').$$
Its zero fibre is exactly $j(E)$ as a sheaf. Indeed, locally $a([v,e])=0$ means $v\in N$, and then $[v,e]=[0,i(v)e]$. Conversely $a([0,e])=0$. The monomorphism property of $j$ makes the local preimage unique, so these preimages glue in the sheaf represented by $E$. This also shows that $j$ identifies $E$ with the scheme-theoretic zero fibre, including on nonreduced test algebras.

source.place: Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319; concretization of its additive-kernel reduction, using Example 2.72 (p.61), Proposition 15.31 (p.318), and Exercise 14-3(a) (p.301).

proof.text: Let $f=a\sigma\in B$ and let $\alpha=\lambda(f)\in k$, using the same coefficient functional as above. Since $\sigma$ is a homomorphism, $f(xy)=f(x)+\psi(x)f(y)$. Apply $\lambda$ in the $y$ variable. The left side is $\alpha$, hence $f(x)=\alpha(1-\psi(x))$. The polynomial $P(T)-\alpha$ is nonconstant, so algebraic closedness gives $v\in k$ with $P(v)=\alpha$.

source.place: Theorem 15.34(d), printed p.319; concretization of its additive-kernel reduction, using Example 2.72 (p.61), Proposition 15.31 (p.318), and Exercise 14-3(a) (p.301).

proof.text:
Conjugate the homomorphism $\sigma$ by $u(-v)$, setting $\sigma'(d)=u(-v)\sigma(d)u(v)$. It still satisfies $r\sigma'=1_D$, and the crossed identity for $a$ gives
$$a(\sigma'(d))=-P(v)+f(d)+\psi(d)P(v)=0.$$
The zero-fibre identification from step 6 therefore factors $\sigma'$ uniquely as $j\circ s$ for a scheme morphism $s:D\to E$. Since $j$ is a group-scheme monomorphism and $\sigma'$ a homomorphism, $s(xy)=s(x)s(y)$ and $s(1)=1$. Finally $q\circ s=rj\circ s=r\sigma'=1_D$.
